When you enable GuardDuty the foundational data sources of VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail logs are also enabled, and those sources cannot be turned off without fully disabling GuardDuty. Runtime Monitoring provides contextual information that allows for more precise findings that can help with targeted remediation compared to the information provided in VPC Flow Logs. When the Runtime Monitoring agent is deployed onto an instance, the GuardDuty service still processes the VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs for that instance. If, at any point in time, an unauthorized user tampers with your security agent or an instance is deployed without the security agent, GuardDuty will continue to use VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs data to monitor for potential threats and suspicious activity, providing you defense in depth to help ensure you have visibility and coverage for detecting threats.\\n\\n> **Note**: GuardDuty doesn\u2019t charge you for processing VPC Flow Logs while the Runtime Monitoring agent is active on an instance\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/get-to-know-amazon-guardduty-runtime-monitoring-for-amazon-ec2/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"GuardDuty foundational data sources\",\"context\":\"## VPC Flow Logs\\n\\nThe VPC Flow Logs feature of Amazon VPC captures information about the IP traffic going to\\nand from network interfaces attached to the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances within your\\nAWS environment.\\n\\nWhen you enable GuardDuty, it immediately starts analyzing VPC flow log data from Amazon EC2\\ninstances within your account. GuardDuty consumes this data through an independent and\\nduplicate stream of flow logs. You don't need to create or configure VPC flow logs\\nin your account for GuardDuty to access this data. This process does not affect any of\\nyour existing flow logs configuration.\\n\\nLambda Protection\\n: Lambda Protection is an optional enhancement to Amazon GuardDuty. Presently,\\n Lambda Network Activity Monitoring includes Amazon VPC flow logs from all Lambda functions for your\\n account, even those logs that don't use VPC networking. To protect your\\n Lambda function from potential security threats, you will need to configure\\n Lambda Protection in your GuardDuty account. For more information, see Lambda Protection.\\n\\nGuardDuty Runtime Monitoring\\n: When you manage the security agent (either manually or through GuardDuty) in EKS Runtime Monitoring\\n or Runtime Monitoring for EC2 instances, and\\n GuardDuty is presently deployed on an Amazon EC2 instance and receives\\n the Collected runtime event\\n types from this instance, GuardDuty will not charge\\n your AWS account for the analysis of VPC flow logs from this Amazon EC2 instance. This helps GuardDuty avoid double usage cost in the account.\\n\\nGuardDuty doesn't manage your flow logs or make them accessible in your account. To manage\\naccess to and retention of your flow logs, you must configure the VPC Flow Logs feature\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_data-sources.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up AWS docs on GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and VPC Flow Log cost interaction"}

{"id": "46248b66-1b27-48c0-972a-f601d80f8371", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Just to be clear: I don't actually have a skill called "GuardDuty cost optimization" in my toolset, so this answer comes from AWS's published documentation rather than that specific source. Here's what the docs say:

**While Runtime Monitoring is active, you don't get double-billed.** For any EC2 instance (or EKS node) running the GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring agent that's actively sending runtime event data:

- GuardDuty **stops charging** for VPC Flow Log processing on that instance, because the runtime agent's event data now provides that coverage.
- GuardDuty still technically processes the VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs in the background for defense-in-depth — but you're not billed for it.
- This shows up as **decreased VPC Flow Log usage** in your GuardDuty CloudWatch usage metrics once Runtime Monitoring is enabled.

**The catch:** this only holds while the agent is actively transmitting data. If the agent stops sending runtime events — say it's tampered with, crashes, or an instance spins up without it — GuardDuty automatically reverts to charging for VPC Flow Log processing on that instance again, so you always stay covered by one method or the other.

Net effect: enabling Runtime Monitoring is generally cost-neutral-to-positive, since it swaps VPC Flow Log processing charges for runtime agent coverage rather than stacking both.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
